 5                    II.     PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

 6   Q5.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

 7   A.    The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to rebut parts of the direct testimonies filed

8          by (i) City of Las Cruces and Don� a Ana County (“CLC/DAC”) witness Mr. Mark

9          Garrett, New Mexico Public Regulation Commission Advisory Staff (“Staff”)

10         witness Ms. Naomi Velasquez, and New Mexico State University (“NMSU”)

11         witness Mr. James Leyko regarding the amount and amortization period of the costs

12         related to the COVID-19 pandemic (“COVID-19”); (ii) Staff witness Mr. Jonah

13         Mauldin regarding the amortization of legacy meters installed after January 1, 2020

14         and removed from service to implement the Advanced Meter System (“AMS”)

15         project; and (iii) CLC/DAC witness Mr. M. Garrett regarding synchronization of

16         post-test year plant additions. I also present changes in rate base to which the

17         Company has agreed and sponsor the revised schedules reflecting changes to which

18         the Company has agreed. Lastly, I present changes in cost of service for items

19         which I sponsored in my amended direct testimony to which the Company has

20         agreed and sponsor the revised schedules reflecting those changes.

21

 1            III.     RESPONSE TO CLC/DAC WITNESS M. GARRETT’S

 2         RECOMMENDATION ON COVID-19 AMORTIZATION PERIOD

 3   Q6.   WHAT IS MR. M. GARRETT’S RECOMMENDATION REGARDING THE

 4         AMORTIZATION PERIOD FOR NET COSTS INCURRED AS A RESULT

 5         OF COVID-19?

 6   A.    Mr. M. Garrett proposes an amortization period of five years for net costs resulting

 7         from COVID-19.

 8

 9   Q7.   WHAT       IS   MR.     GARRET’S          REASONING       FOR     A   FIVE-YEAR

10         AMORTIZATION PERIOD?

11   A.    Mr. M. Garrett states that the COVID-19 costs were incurred over a four-year

12         period and that a five-year period is the typical period that base rates remain in

13         effect. (M. Garrett Direct at 48.)

14

15   Q8.   DO        YOU   AGREE        WITH         MR.   M.    GARRET’S         PROPOSED

16         AMORTIZATION PERIOD FOR COVID-19 COSTS?

17   A.    No. Mr. M. Garrett's five-year period is not supported by the nature of these costs

18         or by sound ratemaking. COVID-19 costs were incurred over a three-year period

19         from March 2020 to May 2023. These costs have already been deferred for five

20         years, and the Company has not earned a return on or a return of these costs for that

21         period.    Extending the recovery period an additional five years would delay

                                                 3
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1         recovery of these costs to ten years after the costs began to be incurred, which is

 2         not reasonable, particularly when considering the Company plans to change the

 3         cadence of its Rate Case filings to every two years for the foreseeable future to keep

 4         pace with EPE’s capital expansion plan, as described in the Rebuttal testimony of

 5         George Novela. A shorter amortization period more closely matches recovery to

 6         the period over which the costs were incurred and avoids further delaying the

 7         Company’s recovery of costs it has already financed.

 8

 9   Q9.   WHAT WOULD THE COMPANY PROPOSE IN RESPONSE TO MR. M.

10         GARRETT’S PROPOSED AMORTIZATION PERIOD FOR COVID-19

11         COSTS?

12   A.    To balance timely cost recovery against customer rate impact, and consistent with

13         the approximately three-year period over which the costs were incurred, the

14         Company is willing to extend the amortization period of COVID-19 costs to three

15         years, which is more consistent with the period over which they were incurred and

16         with the timing of rate case filings discussed by Mr. Novela in his rebuttal

17         testimony.

1               IV.     RESPONSE TO STAFF WITNESS VELASQUEZ

2                                 RECOMMENDATIONS

3    Q10. WHAT ARE MS. VELASQUEZ’S RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING

4         THE NET COSTS INCURRED AS A RESULT OF COVID-19?

 5   A.   Ms. Velasquez recommends that the amount of uncollectible expense incurred by

 6        the Company during COVID-19, which she refers to as bad debt expense, be

 7        reduced by half. Additionally, Ms. Velasquez recommends that the recovery period

 8        for COVID-19 costs be increased to three years.

 9

10   Q11. WHY      DOES      MS.     VELASQUEZ             RECOMMEND         THAT      THE

11        UNCOLLECTIBLE            COSTS     INCURRED         DURING       COVID-19      BE

12        REDUCED BY HALF?

13   A.   Ms. Velasquez recommends reducing the Company's COVID-19 bad debt expense

14        by half, an adjustment of $1,472,375. She states that the Company had a longer

15        period in which to collect uncollectible accounts than other utilities and that the

16        Company should have utilized collection agents and disconnection of service to

17        ensure all avenues of uncollectible accounts were exhausted before these costs are

18        borne by ratepayers. (Velasquez Direct at 14.)

19

20   Q12. DID MS. VELASQUEZ SUBSTANTIATE HER OPINION AND IS IT

21        ACCURATE?

                                               5
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1   A.   No. Ms. Velasquez cited no evidentiary support for her assertion that the Company

 2        failed to exhaust its collection efforts, and as I explain in response to the next

 3        question, the assertion is factually incorrect. The Company pursued all available

 4        collection avenues; many were constrained during the pandemic by government

 5        mandates, not by any lack of effort on the Company’s part.

 6

 7   Q13. WHAT MEASURES DID THE COMPANY TAKE TO RECOVER

 8        ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE WRITTEN-OFF DURING AND AFTER

 9        COVID-19?

10   A.   The Company utilized many collection methods in order to recover accounts

11        receivable balances during COVID-19 including referrals to assistance programs,

12        referrals to budget billing programs, payment notices, customer calls, collection

13        agencies, and disconnection of service. However, many of these methods were

14        ineffective during COVID-19 for several reasons. For example, there were several

15        sustained periods during COVID-19 when the Company was prohibited from

16        disconnecting customers due to non-payment due to mandates by government

17        authorities.   Additionally, referrals to budget billing programs and collection

18        agency efforts were not effective if the customer could not pay due to the loss of

19        employment. The uncollectible balance related to COVID-19 was reduced by all

20        amounts recovered through each of these collection efforts.       Moreover, as I

21        discussed in my direct testimony, after the end of COVID-19, EPE made additional

                                              6
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1        collection efforts which reduced the COVID-19 uncollectible balance by

 2        $4,646,000 on a total Company basis, lowering the New Mexico jurisdictional

 3        balance from $3,952,713 to $2,944,750. These recoveries were subtracted from the

 4        COVID-19 costs requested in this filing, even though they occurred after the

 5        COVID-19 period prescribed by New Mexico. Due to these efforts, the Company

 6        does not agree with Ms. Velasquez’s recommendation to reduce the uncollectible

 7        expense in the COVID-19 costs by half. The Company already pursued and credited

 8        the very collection recoveries Ms. Velasquez contends it should have made, and the

 9        disconnection remedy she references was unavailable during the mandated

10        moratoria.

11

12   Q14. DO YOU AGREE WITH THE RECOVERY PERIOD PROPOSED BY MS.

13        VELASQUEZ FOR COVID-19 COSTS?

14   A.   Yes, as I previously stated, the Company would agree to a three-year recovery

15        period for COVID-19 costs.

16

17                V.      RESPONSE TO STAFF WITNESS LEYKO’S

18                                RECOMMENDATION

19   Q15. WHAT RECOMMENDATION DOES MR. LEYKO MAKE REGARDING

20        THE RECOVERY PERIOD FOR COVID-19 COSTS?




                                              7
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                    CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1   A.   Like Ms. Velasquez, Mr. Leyko recommends a three-year recovery period for

 2        COVID-19 costs.

 3

 4   Q16. DO YOU AGREE WITH THE RECOVERY PERIOD PROPOSED BY MR.

 5        LEYKO FOR COVID-19 COSTS?

 6   A.   Yes, as I previously stated, the Company would agree to a three-year recovery

 7        period for COVID-19 costs.

 8

 9               VI.    RESPONSE TO STAFF WITNESS MAULDIN’S

10                                RECOMMENDATION

11   Q17. WHAT         RECOMMENDATION             DOES      MR.     MAULDIN         MAKE

12        REGARDING THE AMORTIZATION PERIOD OF THE LEGACY

13        METERS INSTALLED AFTER JANUARY 1, 2020?

14   A.   Mr. Mauldin recommends that the recovery period for the legacy meters installed

15        after January 1, 2020 be amortized over a new ten-year period rather than the six-

16        year remaining period proposed by the Company, in order to align with the

17        amortization period for the legacy meters installed prior to January 1, 2020.

18        (Mauldin Direct at 19–20.)

19

20   Q18. DO YOU AGREE WITH THE AMORTIZATION PERIOD PROPOSED BY

21        MR. MAULDIN?

                                              8
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1   A.   Yes. Although the Company’s six-year proposal reflected the remaining portion of

 2        the ten-year amortization period established under the AMS Rider approved in Case

 3        No. 21-00269-UT, the Company does not oppose Mr. Mauldin’s recommendation.

 4        The annual revenue-requirement difference is modest, and the Company will agree

 5        to amortize the legacy meters installed after January 1, 2020 over a ten-year period

 6        to be consistent with the amortization period of the legacy meters installed prior to

 7        January 1, 2020.

 8

 9                  VII.     ADJUSTMENTS TO COST OF SERVICE

10   Q19. WHAT CHANGES HAVE YOU MADE TO THE COST OF SERVICE

11        PROPOSED BY THE COMPANY BASED UPON THE CONCESSIONS

12        AGREED TO IN YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

13   A.   I made three changes to cost of service based on the recommendations as discussed

14        above. The first adjustment to the cost of service is located on line 12, column (c),

15        of Exhibit JIR-3R, which is Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No. 13, as amended for

16        rebuttal adjustments.     This adjustment was made to decrease the annual

17        amortization of the COVID-19 costs from two to three years, and results in a

18        decrease in the annual amortization amount of $679,280 ($2,037,780 original

19        amortization less $1,358,520 revised amortization) on a New Mexico jurisdictional

20        basis.

21

                                                9
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1   Q20. WHAT IS THE SECOND ADJUSTMENT YOU MADE TO COST OF

2         SERVICE?

3    A.   The second adjustment to the cost of service is located on line 15, column (c) of

4         Exhibit JIR-3R. This adjustment was made to decrease the annual amortization of

5         the legacy meters installed after January 1, 2020 from six to ten years, and results

 6        in a decrease in the annual amortization amount of $349,641 ($1,672,773 original

 7        amortization less $1,323,132 revised amortization) on a New Mexico jurisdictional

 8        basis.

 9

10   Q21. WHAT IS THE THIRD ADJUSTMENT YOU MADE TO COST OF

11        SERVICE?

12   A.   The third adjustment to the cost of service is located on page 1, line 1, column (d)

13        of Exhibit CSP-1R, which is Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No. 15 – Depreciation

14        and Amortization Expense as amended for rebuttal adjustments. This change was

15        made to adjust the depreciation expense of steam production units due to the

16        removal of Rio Grande unit 7, Newman unit 1 and Newman unit 2 which are

17        discussed below in my rebuttal testimony. Consistent with the rebuttal testimony

18        of EPE witness John J. Spanos, EPE revised the depreciation expense for these units

19        and reflected the related reclassification within steam production. This adjustment

20        results in a decrease in depreciation expense of $4,313,232 on a Total Company

21        basis and $7,879 on a New Mexico jurisdictional basis. Adjustment No. 15 is

                                     CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1        supported by Schedule H-7, which has been revised to reflect the above adjustments

 2        and is included as Exhibit CSP-2R.

 4                       VIII. ADJUSTMENTS TO RATE BASE

 5   Q22. DID THE COMPANY MAKE AN ADJUSTMENT TO RATE BASE IN

 6        RESPONSE         TO     NMSU         WITNESS       BRIAN       C.    ANDREWS’

 7        RECOMMENDATION REGARDING STEAM GENERATION UNITS

 8        THAT WILL SOON BE RETIRED?

 9   A.   Yes. Mr. Andrews recommends adjustments for certain steam production units

10        scheduled to retire at or near the time new rates become effective. As explained by

11        EPE witness John J. Spanos, given the short remaining lives of these units, an

12        adjustment is appropriate to reflect their expected retirement. Accordingly, EPE

13        removed Rio Grande Unit 7, Newman Unit 1, and Newman Unit 2 from New

14        Mexico rate base and made the related depreciation adjustments described by Mr.

15        Spanos.

16

17   Q23. HOW DID THE COMPANY REFLECT THE REMOVAL OF RIO

18        GRANDE UNIT 7, NEWMAN UNIT 1 AND NEWMAN UNIT 2 FROM

19        RATE BASE?

20   A.   The Company removed the plant in service and accumulated depreciation balances

21        associated with Rio Grande unit 7, Newman unit 1 and Newman unit 2 from rate

                                               11
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

1         base as reflected in revised Workpaper A-3, Adjustments 28, Plant in Service, and

 2        29, Accumulated Depreciation, which are provided as Exhibits CSP-3R and CSP-

 3        4R, respectively, to my rebuttal testimony.

 4

 5   Q24. DID    THE      REMOVAL         OF     THE     PLANT       IN    SERVICE       AND

 6        ACCUMULATED DEPRECIATION BALANCES FOR RIO GRANDE

 7        UNIT 7, NEWMAN UNIT 1 AND NEWMAN UNIT 2 CHANGE RATE

 8        BASE?

 9   A.   No. The difference between the plant in service balance and the accumulated

10        depreciation balance at October 31, 2025, for each of the three units was reallocated

11        to other units in the steam production category, which is consistent with the

12        proposal discussed in the rebuttal testimony of EPE witness John Spanos for the

13        retirement of the three units. Because the reallocation does not change the total

14        steam production reserve, removing the related plant-in-service and accumulated

15        depreciation balances does not result in a net change to total rate base.

16

17   Q25. MR. M. GARRETT CHARACTERIZES EPE’S POST-TEST YEAR PLANT

18        ADDITIONS AS “PIECEMEAL RATEMAKING” MADE WITHOUT

19        OFFSETTING ADJUSTMENTS. DO YOU AGREE?

20   A.   No. Unlike the treatment at issue in EPE’s 2020 Rate Case, Case No. 20-00104-

21        UT, EPE has included its October 2025 plant additions on a fully synchronized

                                               12
                                   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                       CYNTHIA S. PRIETO

 1        basis. As I explained in my Direct Testimony, EPE synchronized the related

 2        accumulated depreciation, depreciation expense, and accumulated deferred income

 3        tax with these plant additions; the ADIT synchronization is sponsored by EPE

 4        witness Henderson. Synchronizing all plant-related balances in this manner is the

 5        standard the Commission has applied when including post-test-period plant in rate

 6        base. Because EPE has reflected these additions together with their offsetting plant-

 7        related balances, the concern Mr. M. Garrett raises about unaccompanied,

 8        piecemeal additions does not apply here.

 9

10   Q26. DO STAFF AND INTERVENORS PROPOSE OTHER ADJUSTMENTS

11        THAT AFFECT EPE’S RATE BASE?

12   A.   Yes. Staff and the intervenors propose adjustments affecting several components

13        of EPE’s rate base that are addressed by other EPE witnesses. Please refer to the

14        rebuttal testimonies of EPE witness Joseph S. Weiss regarding cash working

15        capital; EPE witness Julissa I. Reza regarding regulatory assets and liabilities and

16        the rate-base treatment of deferred regulatory costs; and EPE witness John J.

17        Spanos regarding depreciation rates and related depreciation matters. The rebuttal

18        testimonies of EPE witnesses George Novela and Victor Martinez address issues

19        related to the recovery of post-test-year purchased-capacity costs and the

20        underlying resources.

21
